structural_location.article: ARTICLE I — DECLARATION OF RIGHTS [SECTION 1 - SEC. 32]
structural_location.article_history: Article 1 adopted 1879 (as part of the 1879 California Constitution, the second California Constitution, replacing the 1849 first Constitution)
structural_location.section_1_history_verbatim: (Sec. 1 added Nov. 5, 1974, by Proposition 7. Resolution Chapter 90, 1974.)

verbatim_text.section_1_verbatim_full: All people are by nature free and independent and have inalienable rights. Among these are enjoying and defending life and liberty, acquiring, possessing, and protecting property, and pursuing and obtaining safety, happiness, and privacy.
enumerated_rights_in_section_1: Right to be free and independent (the natural-rights premise)
Inalienable rights (rights that cannot be alienated, surrendered, or taken away)
verbatim_text.doctrinal_significance: Section 1 is the textual root of every rights claim in California state court. It is California's natural-rights premise — the rights enumerated are not granted by government; they pre-exist government and cannot be alienated. The 1974 addition of 'privacy' is the textual foundation of California's distinctive constitutional privacy doctrine, which is more protective than federal privacy doctrine in several respects (Hill v. NCAA 1994, American Academy of Pediatrics v. Lungren 1997, and the entire CMIA framework rest on this clause).

amendment_history.context: California's FIRST Constitution included a Declaration of Rights as Article I. The 1849 Article I § 1 stated the inalienable-rights principle in a different form. California became a state in 1850 with this Constitution.
amendment_history.primary_source_status: NOT YET FETCHED — would require the 1849 Constitution from California State Archives or state library historical collections

amendment_history.context: California's SECOND Constitution (the current one, with many subsequent amendments) was adopted in 1879. Article I § 1 was carried forward with the inalienable-rights formulation but in pre-modern language.

amendment_history.event: MAJOR REVISION. Section 1 was REPLACED with the current text, including the explicit addition of 'privacy' to the enumerated rights. Proposition 7 was a comprehensive update of Article I that also affected many other sections. The right to privacy as an explicit California constitutional right dates from this 1974 amendment.
amendment_history.primary_source_status: NOT YET FETCHED — Proposition 7 ballot pamphlet and resolution text would be in California State Archives

doctrinal_descendant_section.section: Cal. Const. Art. I § 1.1 (added Nov. 8, 2022, by Proposition 1, Resolution Chapter 97, 2022, effective December 21, 2022)
doctrinal_descendant_section.verbatim: The state shall not deny or interfere with an individual's reproductive freedom in their most intimate decisions, which includes their fundamental right to choose to have an abortion and their fundamental right to choose or refuse contraceptives. This section is intended to further the constitutional right to privacy guaranteed by Section 1, and the constitutional right to not be denied equal protection guaranteed by Section 7. Nothing herein narrows or limits the right to privacy or equal protection.
doctrinal_descendant_section.significance: Section 1.1 (2022) explicitly cites Section 1 (1974) as the textual foundation for the constitutional right to privacy. This is the post-Dobbs California response to the federal retreat from substantive due process privacy doctrine: California voters in 2022 added an explicit reproductive-freedom provision that builds on the 1974 privacy amendment. The chain Section 1 (1974) → Section 1.1 (2022) is now in primary source.

rights_audits.what_the_constitution_provides: All people have the inalienable right of acquiring, possessing, and protecting property. Section 1's property-rights guarantee predates and is independent of the federal 5th Amendment Takings Clause.
rights_audits.what_the_record_shows: Per project_house_sale_fraud.md, the steward's interest in 2958 Honeysuckle was diminished from $465K equity to $109K through a process the steward documents as fraudulent. Per project_property_financial_fraud.md, additional property/financial losses are documented. Each loss is, structurally, a deprivation of the right to 'possessing and protecting' property under Section 1.
rights_audits.audit_question: For each documented property loss, was the loss the result of state action (which would invoke Section 1 as a deprivation) or purely private fraud (which would not trigger constitutional protection but would still be actionable under tort and property law)? Where state action is implicated (court orders, recording chain failures, etc.), Section 1 is in play.
rights_audits.audit_status: FLAGGED — bridges to project_house_sale_fraud.md and to the Cal. Civ. § 1213 standard built earlier today.

rights_audits.what_the_constitution_provides: All people have the inalienable right of pursuing and obtaining privacy. The 1974 amendment is the textual foundation of California's distinctive constitutional privacy doctrine.
rights_audits.what_the_record_shows: Multiple branches of the steward's case implicate privacy: (1) medical records disclosed without authorization (per project_medical_fraud_timeline.md, bridges to CMIA § 56.10); (2) communications surveillance (per project_communications_fraud.md, SIM swap/clone interference); (3) conservatorship investigation that may have accessed private records without his knowledge (per project_conservatorship_discovery.md, bridges to CMIA § 56.10(c)(12)).
rights_audits.audit_question: For each documented privacy intrusion, was it the result of state action or state-actor coordination with private parties? Where state action is implicated, Section 1's privacy clause provides a CALIFORNIA constitutional basis (in addition to any federal claims) for redress.
rights_audits.audit_status: CRITICAL — Section 1's privacy clause is the steward's strongest California constitutional anchor. It is more protective than federal privacy doctrine (Hill v. NCAA test is broader than federal substantive-due-process privacy).

rights_audits.what_the_constitution_provides: All people have the inalienable right to enjoying and defending liberty.
rights_audits.what_the_record_shows: Per project_conservatorship_discovery.md and project_conservatorship_breakthrough.md, the steward has discovered evidence of long-standing conservatorship arrangements that potentially constrain his liberty in ways he was not aware of. Per project_june16_2023_timeline.md, the June 16 incident involved physical contact and detention. Per project_familylaw_orchestration.md, custody and family-law processes constrained his liberty across the 16-year case period.
rights_audits.audit_question: For each documented liberty constraint, what was the legal basis? Where the basis is a court order, was the order entered with proper procedural protections? Where the basis is alleged but not formal (e.g., a covert conservatorship), Section 1's liberty clause is invoked at its most fundamental — government cannot constrain liberty without due process.
rights_audits.audit_status: CRITICAL — bridges to procedural-due-process claims under Section 7 (equal protection / due process) and to the federal § 1983 complaint under 14th Amendment substantive due process.

rights_audits.what_the_constitution_provides: All people have the inalienable right of pursuing and obtaining safety.
rights_audits.what_the_record_shows: The entire case file documents a sustained pattern of harm to the steward and his ability to pursue safety. The 'safety' right under Section 1 is unusual in that it is enumerated as a constitutional guarantee, not just a policy preference.
rights_audits.audit_question: Has any state action affirmatively interfered with the steward's pursuit of safety? Has any state actor failed to act in circumstances where the safety guarantee creates an affirmative duty?
rights_audits.audit_status: FLAGGED — California's affirmative-safety doctrine is contested but live; this is an area where the steward's case may push doctrinal frontiers.

rights_audits.what_the_constitution_provides: All people are by nature free and independent AND HAVE INALIENABLE RIGHTS. The word 'inalienable' is doctrinally significant: these rights cannot be surrendered, contracted away, or extinguished by government action. They pre-exist government and constrain it.
rights_audits.what_the_record_shows: If a covert conservatorship has constrained the steward's liberty without his knowledge (per project_conservatorship_breakthrough.md), the inalienability framing is structurally important: a conservatorship the subject doesn't know about cannot be a voluntary surrender of the underlying liberty rights, and any 'consent' inferred from non-objection is structurally invalid because the subject couldn't object to what he didn't know.
rights_audits.audit_question: Have any of the steward's Section 1 rights been treated as alienable by any state actor? The natural-rights premise of Section 1 forecloses that treatment.
rights_audits.audit_status: CRITICAL — doctrinal framing for the entire constitutional theory of the case.

steward_case_relevance_audit.audit_summary: THREE CRITICAL audit items: (1) the privacy clause bridges to medical fraud / conservatorship / surveillance branches of the case; (2) the liberty clause bridges to custody / conservatorship / June 16 detention branches; (3) the inalienability framing structurally forecloses any 'consent' theory for rights the steward didn't know were being implicated. Section 1 is the constitutional foundation under which every California-state-court rights claim in the steward's case can be brought. The 1974 addition of 'privacy' is the most consequential single amendment — it created the textual basis for California's distinctive privacy doctrine and is now the foundation of the steward's medical-privacy and conservatorship-related claims.

five_layer_bar_status.rule: PRESENT — verbatim text extracted with full enumerated-rights breakdown
five_layer_bar_status.reasoning: STRONG — Section 1 is the natural-rights premise of California constitutional law. The reasoning is the entire natural-rights tradition (Locke, Blackstone, the Declaration of Independence) imported into California state constitutional doctrine. The 1974 addition of privacy was specifically motivated by post-Watergate, post-Roe concerns about government surveillance and intrusion into personal life — the Prop 7 ballot argument materials would be the primary-source evidence for this reasoning.
five_layer_bar_status.historical_loss: OUTSTANDING — the documented harms that drove the 1974 privacy amendment (Watergate, government surveillance scandals, the chilling effect on personal autonomy) are well-known but not yet primary-source documented. The 1879 Constitution itself was driven by its own historical losses (the Workingmen's Party's grievances against the railroad and corporate monopolies that had captured California politics under the 1849 Constitution).
five_layer_bar_status.cross_references: PARTIAL — Section 1 connects to every other section of Article I (32 sections in the Declaration of Rights), to Article XX § 22 (oath of office binding officers to the Constitution), and to the entire body of California constitutional case law. § 1.1 (2022 reproductive freedom) explicitly cites § 1 as its textual foundation.
five_layer_bar_status.verifiable_provenance: PRESENT for current form (the entire Article I is captured in one extraction); PARTIAL for evolution layers
